Case_Content:
Man, 64 years old, no significant medical history, presenting with a left colon tumor revealed by subocclusive syndrome.  Thoraco-abdominal CT scan shows a 6 cm colonic mass and two liver metastases in segments II and V measuring 2.2 and 3 cm. CEA: 120 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, MSS. No extra-hepatic disease.
MDT Discussion: Metastases considered primarily resectable, symptomatic colonic lesion is the priority.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront: The two hepatic lesions are small (2.2 cm in segment II and 3 cm in segment V), peripheral, and without vascular or biliary invasion. A limited hepatectomy (wedge or segmentectomy) would leave an adequate future liver remnant. No extra‑hepatic disease is identified. Therefore both the primary colon tumor and the liver metastases are technically resectable without the need for down‑staging therapy.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Proceed to curative‑intent surgery as the first therapeutic step because the colonic lesion is symptomatic and the liver disease is resectable.  
- Preferred approach: simultaneous resection, provided the patient’s performance status is good and operative risk is acceptable.  
   • Laparoscopic (or open) left‑sided colectomy with oncologic lymphadenectomy and primary anastomosis.  
   • In the same session, perform laparoscopic or open parenchymal‑sparing liver resection: wedge resection of segment II lesion and segmentectomy or wedge of segment V lesion, guided by intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm margins and vascular anatomy.  
- If intra‑operative assessment reveals unfavorable liver remnant or technical difficulty, convert to a staged strategy:  
   1. Resection of the primary colon tumor first; recover 2–3 weeks.  
   2. Subsequent liver‑first or delayed hepatic resection, using the same parenchymal‑sparing technique.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant systemic therapy: 6 months of oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX or CAPOX). Given RAS wild‑type status, consider adding anti‑EGFR (cetuximab or panitumumab) in the adjuvant setting only if high‑risk features (e.g., positive nodes, high CEA) are present and multidisciplinary consensus supports it.  
- Surveillance: CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of chest/abdomen every 6 months, colonoscopy at 1 year post‑resection.

Step 3 - Missing data  
No critical information is lacking for a definitive surgical plan. Baseline liver function tests, cardiopulmonary assessment, and future liver remnant volumetry would be obtained pre‑operatively but are not missing for the resectability decision.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two liver metastases (segments II and V, 2.2 cm and 3 cm), bilobar but peripheral, without radiologic evidence of extrahepatic disease. Both lesions appear technically amenable to limited parenchymal-sparing resections (wedge/segmentectomy) with preservation of adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number, small size, and favorable location of metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Priority: management of the symptomatic primary tumor
• The subocclusive presentation makes the left colonic lesion the immediate priority.
• Perform an oncologic left colectomy first (or ileostomy) with lymphadenectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) to treat the obstruction risk and allow safe continuation of the oncologic strategy.
• Alternative : consider a temporary diversion before colectomy according to exact degree of subocclusion.

B. Early systemic therapy after recovery from colectomy
• After the emergent procedure, perform high-resolution liver MRI to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial anatomy. Precise anatomic mapping is required to avoid intra operative surprise 
• Given the high CEA level (120 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT
• Initiate peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI).
• Given the high CEA level (120 ng/mL), the situation suggests biologically active disease; short-course neoadjuvant therapy allows treatment of micrometastases and assessment of tumor biology.
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy depending on MDT decision and tolerance.

C. Liver surgery after restaging (liver-first not indicated here due to symptoms)
• After 2–3 months of chemotherapy, perform high-resolution liver MRI and CT restaging.
• If stability or response is observed, proceed to parenchymal-sparing liver resections: segment II wedge/segmentectomy and segment V wedge/segmentectomy guided by intra-operative ultrasound.
• Aim for R0 margins (>1mm) while preserving maximal liver parenchyma.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Post-hepatectomy therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including pre-operative cycles).
• Close postoperative surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the initially high tumor marker level.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact degree of subocclusion and whether an temporary diversion is required before colectomy.
B. Detailed liver MRI describing vascular and biliary relationships of both metastases to confirm feasibility of parenchymal-sparing resections.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy.
D. Exact location of the left colon tumor (descending vs sigmoid) influencing surgical planning.
E. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
F. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
G. Perform liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 56 years old, incidental discovery of a right colon tumor during a workup for iron deficiency anemia. Thoraco-Abdominal CT scan shows an ileocecal mass and a single 2.5 cm metastasis in segment VI. CEA 35 ng/mL, KRAS mutation present. No other lesions on FDG-PET.
MDT Discussion: Single peripheral metastasis, situation suitable for combined surgical treatment.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
- Category: Resectable upfront  
- Reasoning: The patient has a solitary 2.5 cm peripheral liver metastasis in segment VI amenable to a wedge resection or segmentectomy with clear margins, and a resectable right‑colon primary (ileocecal mass). No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on FDG‑PET, and the lesion size and location do not compromise the future liver remnant. Therefore both the primary tumor and the hepatic metastasis can be removed safely in a single operative session without the need for down‑staging therapy or additional information.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- 1. Complete pre‑operative work‑up:  
  • Full blood count, liver function tests, coagulation profile, and assessment of performance status (ECOG 0‑1).  
  • Colonoscopy with biopsy to confirm histology and obtain tumor‑blocking markers.  
  • Intra‑operative ultrasound of the liver to rule out occult lesions.  
- 2. Surgical plan (simultaneous resection):  
  • Right hemicolectomy with oncologic lymphadenectomy for the primary tumor.  
  • Anatomical segment VI resection (or non‑anatomic wedge) with negative margins (≥1 cm) and preservation of adequate future liver remnant (>30 % in a normal liver).  
  • Use of peri‑operative antibiotics and thromboprophylaxis per protocol.  
- 3. Post‑operative management:  
  • Pathology review to confirm R0 resection of both sites and assess nodal status.  
  • Initiate adjuvant systemic chemotherapy within 6‑8 weeks (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX; consider adding bevacizumab given KRAS mutation, but anti‑EGFR agents are not indicated).  
  • Monitor CEA and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3‑6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  
- 4. Contingency: If intra‑operative ultrasound reveals additional hepatic lesions, convert to staged approach or consider portal vein embolization if future liver remnant is insufficient.

Step 3 – Missing data  
- No critical information is lacking; the provided data are sufficient to formulate a definitive surgical and oncologic plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient has a single 2.5 cm peripheral metastasis in segment VI, no radiologically evident extra hepatic disease, and the lesion is amenable to a non anatomic wedge resection with an expected R0 margin. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered to be potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial anatomy. Precise anatomic mapping is required to avoid intra operative surprise.

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) because the tumor is KRAS mutated (no anti EGFR benefit).
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT).

C. Surgical management
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a simultaneous right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + a segment VI wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. (Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Alternative : consider two-stage surgical resection of primary and liver tumors / consider right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + an image-guided ablation using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals. A level of 35 ng/mL is acceptable but warrants close surveillance

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy. 
B. Potential extension of primary tumor to adjacent organ (abdominal wall, ureter, small bowel)
C. Detailed vascular/biliary relationship of the liver lesion – essential to confirm that a non anatomic resection will achieve clear margins without compromising hepatic inflow/outflow.
G. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
These items should be obtained before finalizing the operative plan.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, history of smoking, presenting with T3N1 upper rectal adenocarcinoma with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis in segment III. Pelvic MRI: limited parietal invasion. CEA 45 ng/mL. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Single resectable metastasis, possibility of coordinated surgical treatment after short-course radiotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectable upfront  
- The 1.8 cm lesion in segment III is peripheral, solitary, and amenable to a wedge resection or segmentectomy with an adequate future liver remnant.  
- The primary upper rectal tumor is T3N1 with limited parietal invasion, suitable for curative resection after short‑course radiotherapy.  
- No extra‑hepatic disease is reported, and the patient’s RAS‑wild type status does not preclude surgery.  
- Therefore both the hepatic and colorectal components meet criteria for immediate surgical resection once neoadjuvant radiotherapy is delivered.  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Short‑course radiotherapy: Deliver 5 × 5 Gy to the rectum over 5 days.  
- Surgical sequencing (within 7–10 days of RT):  
  • Option A – Simultaneous approach: Perform a low anterior resection with total mesorectal excision (laparoscopic or open) together with a laparoscopic segment III liver resection. This minimizes total operative time and hospital stay and avoids two separate recovery periods.  
  • Option B – Staged approach (if operative risk deemed high): First, laparoscopic segment III resection; allow 2–3 weeks for hepatic recovery, then proceed with low anterior resection.  
- Adjuvant systemic therapy: After recovery from surgery, administer 6 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX). RAS‑wild type status permits addition of anti‑EGFR therapy (cetuximab or panitumumab) if high‑risk features are identified.  
- Surveillance: Serial CEA measurements and imaging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- No essential data are lacking for a reliable resectability assessment and management plan. (If needed, confirm performance status, liver function tests, and volumetric FLR, but current information is sufficient.)
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis located in segment III. The lesion seems technically amenable to a parenchymal-sparing resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for solitary, small metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial liver anatomy. 

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab or cetuximab)
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy depending on MDT strategy.
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver and rectum MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control for both

C. Management of the rectal primary (oncologic priority)
• Given the T3N1 upper rectal tumor with limited parietal invasion, long-course radiotherapy is appropriate to optimize local control and allow coordinated surgical planning.

D. Coordinated surgical strategy
• Initiate doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX) during the waiting period following radiotherapy. This period treats potential micrometastatic disease and tests tumor biology.
• Consider image-guided ablation of the single segment III lesion using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)
• After restaging with high-resolution liver MRI and pelvic imaging,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segment III metastasis with follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segment III metastasis followed with strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : liver-first resection or ablation of the single segment III metastasis, then rectal resection after appropriate recovery, using a staged or synchronous strategy : oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
– Parenchymal-sparing segment III wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins.
Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, influencing the type of rectal resection and anastomotic risk.
B. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT . Chest CT.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
D. Detailed relationship of the liver lesion to segment III vascular structures on liver MRI.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 72 years old, discovery at abdominal CT scan of a transverse colon adenocarcinoma, CEA 410 ng/mL, three liver metastases (segments IV, V and VI) measuring 2 to 3 cm. Liver MRI: partial contact with the right portal branch without invasion. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Primarily resectable metastases, simple liver surgery possible.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront: All three hepatic lesions are ≤3 cm, show only partial contact with the right portal branch without radiologic invasion, and are amenable to limited parenchymal resection (segmentectomy/wedge). No extra‑hepatic disease is reported, and the primary transverse colon tumor is presumed resectable by standard colectomy. Therefore, curative‑intent surgery can be planned immediately without mandatory pre‑operative down‑staging.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• 1. Baseline work‑up: confirm adequate hepatic reserve (ICG clearance or volumetry), assess performance status (ECOG 0‑1), and obtain full staging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, colonoscopy report for T/N stage).  
• 2. Multimodal peri‑operative plan:  
   – a. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX + bevacizumab) for 2–3 months to treat micrometastatic disease, verify tumor biology, and potentially lower CEA.  
   – b. Restaging MRI/CT after chemotherapy to confirm that all lesions remain resectable and that no new extra‑hepatic sites have appeared.  
   – c. If liver volume is adequate (future liver remnant ≥ 30 % in a normal liver), proceed to simultaneous resection: right hemicolectomy (or extended right hemicolectomy) for the transverse colon primary plus limited hepatic resection (segment IV, V, VI) using parenchymal‑sparing techniques.  
   – d. If FLR is borderline, consider portal vein embolization before the liver stage or adopt a staged approach (colon first, then liver).  
   – e. Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy to complete a total of 6 months of systemic therapy.  
   – f. Surveillance: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the liver every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

Step 3 - Missing data  
No critical data are lacking for a definitive resectability judgment; however, the following information would refine peri‑operative planning:  
• Exact T and N stage of the colon primary (to confirm resectability and need for lymphadenectomy).  
• Patient’s performance status and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
• Baseline liver function and volumetric assessment of future liver remnant.  
• Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease on full staging (e.g., lung, peritoneum).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with three liver metastases located in segments IV, V, and VI (2–3 cm), confined to the right liver and central segments. MRI shows only partial contact with the right portal branch and no evidence of vascular invasion. These lesions appear technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections or anatomicalm resection while preserving adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number and size of metastases with preserved vascular structures, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative systemic therapy (strongly recommended)
• The very high CEA level (410 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation suggest biologically aggressive disease.
• Given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL), perform chest CT scan and high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.

B. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of the lesions to the right portal branch and confirm maintained resectability.
• Evaluate future liver remnant (FLR) if right hepatectomy of considered.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform combined parenchymal-sparing resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segment IV wedge/segmentectomy.
– Segment V and VI wedge resections.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Management of the primary tumor
• Transverse colectomy of extended right colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT and chest CT scan.
B. Detailed vascular mapping on MRI to confirm absence of true portal invasion.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) calculation in case of right hepatectomy.F. Circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. 
D. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 59 years old, T3N1 sigmoid colon tumor associated with four peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, VIII) at the abdominal CT scan. Maximum size: 2.9 cm. CEA 200 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, HER2 negative.
MDT Discussion: Primarily resectable lesions, no vascular or extra-hepatic involvement.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront: All hepatic lesions are peripheral, ≤3 cm, located in segments II, III, V and VIII without vascular invasion, and the primary sigmoid tumor is surgically accessible. A parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy (multiple wedge resections or segmental resections) can achieve negative margins while preserving an adequate future liver remnant (>30 % in a normal liver). No extra‑hepatic disease is identified. Therefore the disease is technically resectable without the need for down‑staging therapy.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Simultaneous curative resection: Perform a laparoscopic or open sigmoid colectomy with primary anastomosis together with a parenchymal‑sparing liver resection (wedge/segmental resections of segments II, III, V, VIII) aiming for R0 margins.  
• Intra‑operative assessment: Use intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion location, number and to guide resection margins; obtain frozen sections of margins if needed.  
• Post‑operative systemic therapy: Start adjuvant chemotherapy within 4–6 weeks after surgery. Preferred regimen is 6 months of FOLFOX (or CAPOX) combined with an anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given the RAS‑wild‑type status, to address micrometastatic disease and the high pre‑operative CEA level.  
• Surveillance: Serial CEA measurements every 3 months for the first 2 years, contrast‑enhanced liver MRI or CT every 6 months, and colonoscopic evaluation at 1 year post‑resection.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
No critical information is lacking to make a definitive surgical plan. The only ancillary data that would further refine peri‑operative risk assessment are:  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume (CT volumetry) and liver function tests (ICG clearance, bilirubin, albumin).  
- Patient’s performance status and cardiopulmonary reserve.  
- Staging of the chest (CT) to definitively exclude pulmonary metastases.  
These items are desirable but not essential to proceed with the recommended strategy.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, and VIII), all smaller than 3 cm, without vascular involvement or extrahepatic disease. The distribution is bilobar but the lesions are technically amenable to multiple parenchymal-sparing resections while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number, small size, and peripheral location of metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative systemic therapy (recommended)
• The elevated CEA level (200 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.
• Given the high CEA level (200 ng/mL), perform chest CT scan and high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI).
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy according to MDT decision.
• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.

B. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform multiple wedge/segmental resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segments II–III resections (left lateral section wedges).
– Segment V wedge resection.
– Segment VIII wedge resection.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Management of the primary tumor
• If the sigmoid tumor has not yet been resected, a simultaneous sigmoid colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis can be considered, provided the patient’s condition allows combined surgery.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT and chest CT scan.
B. Detailed liver MRI describing vascular and biliary relationships of each lesion.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy.
F. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 63 years old, right-sided T4N2M1 colon cancer, two liver metastases in segments II and IVa (3 and 4 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. Liver MRI: middle hepatic vein preserved. CEA 95 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Technically resectable metastases, with priority given to controlling the primary tumor.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
- Both hepatic lesions are ≤4 cm, located in segments II and IVa, and the middle hepatic vein is preserved, allowing a parenchymal‑sparing resection with an adequate future liver remnant.  
- No extra‑hepatic disease is reported on the thoraco‑abdominal CT.  
- The primary colon tumor is technically resectable (right‑sided T4 lesion amenable to right hemicolectomy).  
- The patient’s age (63) and presumed functional status do not preclude major abdominal surgery.  
Therefore the disease meets anatomical and functional criteria for immediate surgical resection without mandatory pre‑operative down‑staging.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Initial surgical control of the primary tumor  
   - Perform a right hemicolectomy with en‑bloc resection of the T4 lesion, aiming for R0 margins.  
   - If intra‑operative assessment shows no need for multivisceral resection beyond standard bowel resection, proceed without additional organ removal.  

2. Post‑operative recovery and systemic therapy  
   - Allow 4–6 weeks for postoperative recovery.  
   - Initiate peri‑operative systemic chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months to treat micrometastatic disease and to assess tumor biology. KRAS mutation excludes anti‑EGFR agents.  

3. Re‑assessment of hepatic disease  
   - Repeat contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT) after chemotherapy to confirm that the two metastases remain resectable and to evaluate any new lesions.  

4. Liver resection  
   - If still resectable, perform a parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy: segment II and segment IVa wedge/segmentectomies preserving the middle hepatic vein, ensuring an adequate future liver remnant (>30 % in a normal liver).  
   - Aim for R0 margins; intra‑operative ultrasound to delineate lesion borders.  

5. Adjuvant therapy  
   - Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre‑operative courses) after liver surgery, adjusting based on postoperative pathology and tolerance.  

6. Surveillance  
   - Serial CEA measurements every 3 months and imaging (CT or MRI) every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually, to detect recurrence early.

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- Baseline liver function tests and volumetric assessment of future liver remnant.  
- Details of T4 invasion (whether adjacent organ involvement requires multivisceral resection).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease not captured on the current CT (e.g., peritoneal implants, lung nodules).  
- Pre‑operative laboratory values (CBC, coagulation profile, renal function).  
- Patient’s preferences regarding staged versus simultaneous surgery.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two liver metastases located in segments II and IVa (3 and 4 cm), without evidence of extrahepatic disease. MRI confirms preservation of the middle hepatic vein and no major vascular invasion. Both lesions are technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections (in case of effective tumor shrinkage with neoadjuvant therapy) or left hepatectomy with preservation of the middle hepatic vein. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number and favorable anatomical location of metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Priority: control of the primary tumor
• The elevated CEA level (95 ng/mL) and right-sided T4N2 colon cancer represents locally advanced disease and is the immediate oncologic priority.
• Given the high CEA level (95 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Assess potential extension of primary tumor to adjacent organ (abdominal wall, ureter, small bowel, duodenum)
• 3 options
-	Perform an oncologic right hemicolectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis, first to control the primary tumor and prevent local complications.
-	Perform an derivation ileostomy first to control the primary tumor and prevent local complications during chemotherapy.
-	Initiate peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).

B. Early systemic therapy after recovery
• Initiate peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• This period allows treatment of micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Liver surgery after restaging
• After 2–3 months of chemotherapy, perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan restaging.
• If tumor response is observed on primary cancer : proceed to oncologic right hemicolectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis
• If tumor response is observed on liver metastases, proceed to parenchymal-sparing resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segment II wedge/segmentectomy.
– Segment IVa wedge/segmentectomy.
• If stability or progression is observed, proceed to anatomic left hepatectomy preserving the middle hepatic vein guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Step 3 – Critical missing information

Man, 47 years old,at the abdominal CT scan T3N0 upper rectal cancer with three liver metastases (segments VI, VII and VIII), sizes 1-2 cm. CEA 60 ng/mL, RAS wild-type. No other lesions on PET.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar metastases primarily resectable, considered for combined treatment after short-course pelvic radiotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: The liver metastases are technically resectable (small, confined to segments VI‑VIII) and the primary rectal tumor is resectable after neoadjuvant therapy. However, definitive surgery cannot be performed immediately because a short‑course pelvic radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) is required before any operative intervention. This prerequisite makes the case “Potentially resectable.”

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Short‑course pelvic radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) to the upper rectal tumor, completed within one week.  
• Immediately after radiotherapy, initiate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR antibody such as cetuximab, given RAS wild‑type) to treat micrometastatic disease and to confirm stability of liver lesions.  
• Restaging with contrast‑enhanced liver MRI and pelvic MRI after chemotherapy to verify that the three hepatic lesions remain ≤2 cm and that the rectal tumor has responded (no progression).  
• If restaging confirms resectability, proceed with a liver‑first approach: perform a parenchymal‑sparing right posterior sectorectomy (or limited right hepatectomy) preserving ≥30 % future liver remnant, ensuring negative margins (R0).  
• Within 4–6 weeks after hepatic surgery (or concurrently if operative risk is acceptable), perform low anterior resection with total mesorectal excision for the rectal primary, preserving sphincter function.  
• Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (additional 2–3 cycles) to complete a total of 8–9 cycles, based on final pathology and patient recovery.  
• Ongoing surveillance with CEA, 6‑monthly CT or MRI, and colonoscopy per standard guidelines.

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Baseline liver function tests and indocyanine‑green clearance or other assessment of hepatic reserve.  
• Quantitative future liver remnant (FLR) volume calculation from imaging.  
• Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
• Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge and involvement of the mesorectal fascia on MRI.  
• Details of vascular anatomy (portal/hepatic veins) around segments VI‑VIII.  
• Pre‑operative serum albumin, bilirubin, and platelet count.  

These data are essential to finalize the surgical plan and to confirm that the patient can safely tolerate the proposed staged or simultaneous resections.

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, history of hypertension, discovery of left colon cancer and a single 2.7 cm liver metastasis in segment IVb at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 40 ng/mL. BRAF wild-type, MSS.
MDT Discussion: Isolated metastasis, anatomically favorable for a single resection.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
- Single 2.7 cm metastasis in segment IVb is anatomically amenable to a limited liver resection with adequate margins.  
- No evidence of additional intra‑ or extra‑hepatic disease on the provided CT.  
- Patient’s only comorbidity is controlled hypertension; no reported hepatic dysfunction or insufficient future liver remnant.  
- Therefore the liver lesion can be removed immediately without prerequisite systemic therapy or further diagnostic work‑up.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Pre‑operative work‑up  
  • Complete blood count, liver panel, coagulation profile, and assessment of functional liver reserve (ICG clearance or indocyanine green retention if available).  
  • Chest CT to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
  • Colonoscopic staging (tumor depth, nodal status) and MRI pelvis if needed for local staging.  
- Surgical plan  
  • Perform a left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection with adequate lymphadenectomy).  
  • Concomitant liver resection: anatomical segment IVb resection or wedge excision ensuring ≥1 cm radial margin; intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion location and exclude occult disease.  
  • Consider simultaneous resection given limited liver disease and acceptable operative risk; otherwise stage with colon resection first, followed by liver resection within 4–6 weeks.  
- Adjuvant therapy  
  • Post‑operative systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX or CAPOX) as per stage IV colon cancer guidelines, given BRAF wild‑type, MSS status.  
  • Consider adding targeted therapy (e.g., anti‑EGFR) only if RAS wild‑type and high‑risk features; otherwise standard regimen is appropriate.  
- Surveillance  
  • CEA monitoring every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
  • Imaging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis) every 6 months for 2 years, then annually.

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Exact T and N stage of the primary colon tumor.  
- Baseline performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky).  
- Detailed liver function tests and volumetric assessment of future liver remnant.  
- Confirmation of absence of extra‑hepatic disease beyond the reported CT (e.g., chest imaging).  
These data would refine peri‑operative risk assessment but are not prohibitive to the recommended plan.

The lesion is anatomically favorable for a a non anatomic wedge resection with an expected R0 margin. A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI to confirm the relationship of the lesion to segment IVb vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection.

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to treat potential micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology, however the KRAS status is unknown.

• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT. 

C. Surgical management
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a simultaneous left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + a segment IVb wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals.

A. K-Ras status, grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy. 
B. Potential extension of primary tumor to adjacent organ (abdominal wall, ureter, small bowel)

MDT Discussion: Limited and accessible liver involvement, no indication for upfront chemotherapy.

- The primary sigmoid lesion is T3N1, amenable to standard oncologic colectomy with clear margins.

- No essential data are lacking to make a reliable resection and treatment recommendation. The case provides sufficient information on tumor burden, location, and baseline oncologic considerations.

Woman, 65 years old, simultaneous discovery of a right colon adenocarcinoma and a 3 cm liver metastasis in segment VII at the abdominal CT scan CEA 70 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Deep but resectable metastasis, discussion of simultaneous versus sequential surgery.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
Reasoning: The patient has a solitary 3 cm metastasis confined to segment VII, which is technically amenable to a limited hepatic resection (segmentectomy or wedge) with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. No extra‑hepatic disease is reported, the primary right‑colon lesion is resectable by standard oncologic right hemicolectomy, and the patient’s age (65) and RAS‑wild‑type status do not preclude surgery. Therefore the disease meets criteria for immediate curative resection without mandatory pre‑operative down‑staging.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Pre‑operative work‑up  
   • Complete blood count, liver panel, coagulation profile, CEA trend.  
   • Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI or CT volumetry to confirm FLR >30 % (or >40 % if steatosis/fibrosis).  
   • Chest CT to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
   • Cardiopulmonary assessment (ASA, ECOG) to confirm fitness for combined procedure.  

2. Surgical plan (simultaneous resection) – preferred if FLR and performance status are adequate  
   • Right hemicolectomy with oncologic lymphadenectomy (D3) for the primary tumor.  
   • Anatomical segment VII resection (segmentectomy) or non‑anatomic wedge resection with negative margins (≥1 cm) and intra‑operative ultrasound guidance.  
   • Use of Pringle maneuver only if needed; aim for minimal ischemia time.  

3. Post‑operative systemic therapy  
   • Start adjuvant chemotherapy within 6–8 weeks (6 months total). Preferred regimen: CAPOX (capecitabine + oxaliplatin) or FOLFOX.  
   • Because the tumor is RAS‑wild‑type and CEA is elevated, consider adding an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab) to the oxaliplatin‑based regimen for high‑risk features (e.g., T4 or N2 disease) after multidisciplinary review.  

4. Surveillance  
   • CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.  
   • Contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of chest, abdomen, pelvis at 6‑month intervals for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Alternative (if FLR or comorbidities are limiting): staged approach – first resect the colon primary, recover, then perform liver resection after a short course (2–3 months) of neoadjuvant chemotherapy to further downsize any occult disease and assess tumor biology.

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Detailed liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin) and quantitative future liver remnant volume.  
• Performance status / comorbidity profile (ASA, cardiac/pulmonary reserve).  
• Exact staging of the primary tumor (T‑stage, N‑stage, presence of lymphovascular invasion).  
• Chest imaging to rule out pulmonary metastases.  
• Assessment of steatosis or fibrosis that could affect hepatic reserve.  

These data are required to confirm that simultaneous resection is safe and to fine‑tune the adjuvant systemic regimen.

- Initiate conversion systemic therapy with FOLFOX plus bevacizumab; plan for 3–6 months of treatment, reassessing every 8–12 weeks with contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI.  
- Perform baseline and interval liver volumetry to estimate future liver remnant (FLR); if FLR is <30 % of total liver volume, schedule right portal vein embolization after an adequate response to chemotherapy.  
- Restage disease after chemotherapy: if all lesions have regressed to ≤2 cm and no new extra‑hepatic sites are identified, re‑evaluate resectability with a multidisciplinary liver‑surgery team.  
- If resectability is confirmed, consider a two‑stage hepatectomy or a single‑stage extended right hepatectomy with intra‑operative ultrasound guidance, depending on lesion distribution and FLR.  
- Plan primary tumor management: if the colon primary is asymptomatic, defer right hemicolectomy until after hepatic resection (liver‑first approach). If symptoms or obstruction develop, perform simultaneous or staged colectomy as clinically indicated.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., continuation of FOLFOX or switch to CAPOX) for a total of 6 months of systemic therapy, adjusted for pathologic response and margin status.  
- Ongoing surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

- Quantitative future liver remnant volume calculation.  
- Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities that may limit chemotherapy or surgery.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum) on full staging (PET‑CT or chest CT).

- Patient’s preferences regarding treatment intensity and surgical timing.

Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has bilobar liver metastases that currently preclude a safe, curative hepatectomy because the future liver remnant would be insufficient and one lesion abuts the right hepatic vein. The MDT plan explicitly requires a course of systemic chemotherapy (conversion therapy) and repeat imaging before a definitive surgical decision can be made. The need for this pre‑operative down‑staging constitutes a specific prerequisite action, fulfilling the criteria for the “Potentially resectable” category.

- Initiate systemic conversion chemotherapy: preferred regimen FOLFOXIRI (5‑FU, leucovorin, oxaliplatin, irinotecan) combined with bevacizumab, given RAS‑wild type status; alternatively, FOLFOX or FOLFIRI plus anti‑EGFR (cetuximab) if contraindications to bevacizumab exist.

   • Consider a two‑stage hepatectomy (first stage portal vein embolization of the right liver to hypertrophy left segments II‑III, followed by delayed right‑sided resection) if FLR remains marginal.  
   • If FLR is sufficient after down‑staging, perform a single‑stage, anatomic or non‑anatomic resection of all four metastases, preserving the right hepatic vein or reconstructing it if necessary.  
- Simultaneous or staged resection of the primary sigmoid tumor:  
   • If the primary is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) or at high risk, resect sigmoid colon first (open or laparoscopic segmental colectomy).  
   • If asymptomatic, consider simultaneous colorectal and liver resection after down‑staging, provided operative risk is acceptable.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (additional 6–8 cycles) to consolidate response and address micrometastatic disease.  
- Ongoing surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3–6 months for the first 2 years.

- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, albumin, INR) and Child‑Pugh classification.  
- Quantitative volumetric assessment of the future liver remnant.  
- Exact size (diameter) of each hepatic lesion and degree of vascular involvement (right hepatic vein encasement vs. abutment).  
- Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities that may affect chemotherapy tolerance or surgical risk.  
- Presence or absence of additional extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., lung, peritoneum).  
- Details of the primary tumor’s symptomatology (obstruction, bleeding) to guide timing of colorectal resection.

• If perspectives of curative option for liver metastases (i.e. intensive chemotherapy of intra-arterial chemotherapy), perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) should be coordinated according to response and patient condition (ideally after liver surgery).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for colectomy.

G. If insufficient response
• Continue systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all 7 lesions specially for the central lesions with detailed vascular and hilar relationships on liver MRI.
B. Baseline future liver remnant (FLR) estimation in case of two-stage strategy with major hepatectomy.
E. Presence or absence of any extrahepatic disease on full staging.
F. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, right T4aN2 colon cancer, ten bilobar liver metastases (1-4 cm) at the abdominal CT scan, CEA 1350 ng/mL, BRAF wild-type. Liver MRI: contact with IVC and left portal branch.
MDT Discussion: Not initially resectable, induction therapy planned before re-evaluation.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has ten bilobar liver metastases, some abutting the IVC and the left portal branch, which precludes a safe, curative‑intent hepatectomy at presentation. The MDT has already planned induction systemic therapy, indicating that tumor downsizing or conversion is required before a definitive surgical decision can be made. The need for this pre‑operative treatment satisfies the definition of “Potentially resectable” (a specific prerequisite action must be completed).

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Initiate intensive systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) for 3–4 months, given the high tumor burden and BRAF wild‑type status.  
- Obtain baseline and interval imaging (contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with diffusion, CT chest/abdomen) after 2–3 months to assess radiologic response and to re‑measure the relationship of lesions to vascular structures.  
- If ≥70 % response with reduction of lesions to ≤4 cm and conversion to a unilobar or limited bilobar distribution, proceed to multidisciplinary re‑evaluation for surgical planning.  
- Evaluate future liver remnant (FLR) volume using volumetric CT; if FLR <30 % of total liver in a normal liver or <40 % in a steatotic liver, schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) of the diseased hemiliver to hypertrophy the FLR.  
- Plan a staged hepatic resection:  
   • First stage – right (or right‑trisection) hepatectomy after adequate FLR hypertrophy, preserving left lateral segment.  
   • If residual disease remains in the left lateral segment, consider a second‑stage limited resection or ablation.  
- Simultaneous or sequential resection of the primary right colon cancer:  
   • If the primary is asymptomatic, defer colectomy until after hepatic resection to reduce operative stress.  
   • If symptomatic (obstruction/bleeding), perform right hemicolectomy first, followed by systemic therapy and hepatic surgery.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (same regimen or continuation of maintenance bevacizumab) for 3–6 months, tailored to pathologic response and margin status.  
- If after induction therapy the hepatic disease remains unresectable (persistent bilobar disease, inadequate FLR, or vascular encasement), discuss alternative strategies: hepatic arterial infusion pump chemotherapy, stereotactic body radiotherapy, or enrollment in a clinical trial; continue systemic therapy as palliative intent.

Step 3 – Missing data  
- KRAS/NRAS mutational status (to confirm eligibility for anti‑EGFR therapy).  
- Baseline performance status (ECOG/WHO) and comorbidities influencing surgical risk.  
- Detailed liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) and assessment of underlying liver disease (steatosis, fibrosis).  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume measurement.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes) on staging CT/PET.  
- Symptoms related to the primary tumor (obstruction, bleeding) and need for urgent colectomy.  
- Patient’s preferences regarding aggressive conversion therapy versus palliative approach.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with ten bilobar liver metastases (1–4 cm) with contact to the inferior vena cava and the left portal branch, without reported extrahepatic disease. The very high tumor burden, bilobar distribution, and involvement of major vascular structures make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not feasible with an upfront surgical approach. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Given the high CEA level (1350 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT and a chest CT scan
• Perform enhanced multi-phase CT-scan to detect potential extension of primary tumor to adjacent organ (abdominal wall, ureter, small bowel)

B. Induction (conversion) systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Initiate intensive systemic chemotherapy as planned : triplet chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab).
• KRAS status is unknown
• BRAF wild-type does not modify the surgical indication.
• The objective is major tumor downsizing, reduction in lesion number/volume, and clearance from the IVC and left portal branch.

C. Close radiologic monitoring
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to assess response, particularly the evolution of vascular contact.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment response.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Marked reduction in tumor burden.
– Separation from the IVC and left portal branch.
– Feasibility of staged or parenchymal-sparing resections with adequate future liver remnant.

E. Potential surgical strategies if response is favorable
• Two-stage hepatectomy or extensive parenchymal-sparing resections with or without combined tumor ablation guided by imaging depending on response pattern.
• Portal vein embolization / venous deprivation / ALPPS may be required if major hepatectomy becomes necessary.

F. Management of the primary tumor
• Right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) should be coordinated according to response and patient condition (ideally after liver surgery).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for colectomy.

G. If insufficient response
• Continue systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all 10 lesions with detailed vascular and biliary relationships and detailed relationship of lesions to the IVC and portal structures on liver MRI.
B. Baseline future liver remnant (FLR) estimation in case of two-stage strategy with major hepatectomy.
C. chest CT scan
E. Presence or absence of any extrahepatic disease on full staging.
F. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
G. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 50 years old, T3N1M1 rectal cancer, five liver metastases (segments II, III, IVa, VI, VII), max size 4.1 cm. CEA 370 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Extensive bilobar involvement, possibility of conversion depending on response to chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
- Category: Potentially resectable  
- Reasoning: The patient has five bilobar liver metastases up to 4.1 cm, which can be technically removed only if (a) sufficient future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved (≥30 % of healthy liver, ≥40 % after chemotherapy‑associated liver injury) and (b) the lesions respond to systemic therapy to allow margin‑negative resection. Both requirements demand pre‑operative interventions (systemic chemotherapy ± portal vein embolization or staged hepatectomy). Therefore the case is not immediately resectable but may become resectable after these prerequisite steps.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy appropriate for KRAS‑mutated colorectal cancer (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) for 2–3 months, aiming for tumor shrinkage and assessment of disease biology.  
- Concurrently deliver standard neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for the T3N1 rectal primary (long‑course 50.4 Gy with 5‑FU‑based radiosensitizer).  
- Perform restaging with contrast‑enhanced MRI or CT of the liver and pelvis, plus volumetric analysis of the FLR.  
- If imaging shows ≥30 % reduction in total hepatic tumor volume and FLR is adequate, proceed to liver surgery:  
   • Option A – Two‑stage hepatectomy: first stage resect lesions in the future liver remnant (segments II/III) and perform portal vein embolization of the contralateral lobe; second stage after hypertrophy (≈4–6 weeks) to clear remaining lesions (segments IVa, VI, VII).  
   • Option B – ALPPS (Associating Liver Partition and Portal vein Ligation for Staged hepatectomy) if FLR hypertrophy is expected to be insufficient with PVE alone and patient fitness permits.  
- After completion of liver surgery, schedule definitive rectal resection (low anterior resection or abdominoperineal resection) 6–8 weeks later, once hepatic recovery is confirmed.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., continuation of the same regimen) for a total of 6 months of systemic therapy, adjusted to response and tolerance.  
- Throughout, monitor CEA trends and consider repeat imaging at 3‑month intervals for early detection of recurrence.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, AST/ALT, INR, platelet count) and assessment of underlying liver disease (steatosis, fibrosis).  
- Quantitative volumetric measurement of the future liver remnant.  
- Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities that could affect tolerance of intensive chemotherapy or major hepatic surgery.  
- Detailed anatomic relationship of each metastasis to major hepatic vessels and biliary structures.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease beyond the rectal primary (e.g., lung, peritoneum).  
- Patient’s preferences regarding staged versus simultaneous resections.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with five bilobar liver metastases (segments II, III, IVa, VI, VII), up to 4.1 cm. The bilobar distribution and tumor burden make a complete R0 parenchymal-sparing resection unlikely with an upfront approach while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Given the high CEA level (370 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT and chest CT scan
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI to define exact segmental distribution of all lesions with detailed vascular and biliary relationships. 

B. Conversion systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Initiate intensive doublet or triplet chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) as discussed in MDT.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• The objective is tumor downsizing, reduction of bilobar tumor burden.

C. Early radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan every 2 months to assess:
– Response of liver metastases and primary cancer.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment response.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Significant reduction in lesion size and number.
– Separation from the middle hepatic vein.
– Feasibility of staged or parenchymal-sparing resections and/or ablation with adequate future liver remnant.

E. Potential surgical strategies if response is favorable
• Two-stage hepatectomy or combined parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• Portal vein embolization / venous deprivation / ALPPS may be required if major hepatectomy becomes necessary.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

F. Management of the rectal primary
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles.
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.

F. If insufficient response
• Continue systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all 5 lesions with detailed vascular and biliary relationships on liver MRI.
B. Baseline future liver remnant (FLR) estimation in case of two-stage strategy with major hepatectomy.
C. chest CT scan
E. Presence or absence of any extrahepatic disease on full staging.
F. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
G. Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, and circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI influencing surgical approach and anastomotic risk.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 62 years old, operated 4 years ago for right colon adenocarcinoma (T3N1M0), no initial recurrence. Surveillance: CEA 180 ng/mL. At the thoraco-abdominal CT scan: two liver lesions segments V and VIII, 2.8 and 3.2 cm. Liver MRI confirms no other foci. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Isolated metachronous metastases, anatomically accessible, good general condition.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
The patient has two isolated liver metastases (2.8 cm in segment V and 3.2 cm in segment VIII) with no extra‑hepatic disease on high‑quality CT/MRI, good performance status, and preserved liver parenchyma. Anatomically the lesions are amenable to a limited right‑lobe resection (segmentectomy or non‑anatomic wedge) while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. No oncologic or functional contraindication is evident, therefore surgery can be offered immediately.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Pre‑operative work‑up  
   • Verify liver biochemistry, bilirubin, INR, platelet count, and calculate indocyanine‑green clearance or perform volumetric CT to confirm FLR ≥ 30 % (≥ 40 % if steatosis/fibrosis).  
   • Review cardiopulmonary assessment and ECOG status; ensure fitness for major hepatectomy.  
   • Obtain baseline CEA trend and repeat imaging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis) within 4 weeks to rule out occult extra‑hepatic disease.  

2. Surgical plan (first definitive therapy)  
   • Perform a right posterior sectionectomy (segments V‑VIII) or two separate parenchymal‑sparing segmentectomies, guided by intra‑operative ultrasound to achieve R0 margins (≥ 1 cm).  
   • Use Pringle maneuver selectively; consider low‑central venous pressure anesthesia to minimize blood loss.  
   • Send frozen sections of margins intra‑operatively; achieve negative margins before closure.  

3. Post‑operative systemic therapy (adjuvant)  
   • Start 6 months of oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab (KRAS‑mutated disease precludes anti‑EGFR).  
   • If postoperative pathology shows high‑risk features (≥ 4 cm, lymphovascular invasion, positive margins), consider intensifying to 8 months or adding a second‑line agent per multidisciplinary consensus.  

4. Surveillance  
   • CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.  
   • Contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the chest/abdomen every 6 months for 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Quantitative liver function assessment (bilirubin, albumin, INR, platelet count, ICG clearance) and volumetric measurement of the future liver remnant.  
• Detailed performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities (cardiovascular, pulmonary, diabetes).  
• Prior exposure to systemic chemotherapy (if any) and tolerance.  
• Exact CEA trajectory over time (baseline vs. current).  
• Confirmation of absence of extra‑hepatic disease on recent chest imaging (CT or PET‑CT).  

These data are needed to finalize peri‑operative risk assessment and to tailor the adjuvant chemotherapy regimen.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two metachronous liver metastases in segments V and VIII (2.8 and 3.2 cm), without evidence of extrahepatic disease. Both lesions are peripherally located in the right liver and technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited, metachronous, anatomically favorable metastases, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Given the high CEA level (180 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Preoperative systemic therapy (recommended)
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI).
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.
• Given the metachronous presentation after a long disease-free interval and the limited number of lesions, immediate surgical resection is appropriate without mandatory neoadjuvant chemotherapy cou ld be considered

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

D. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, two wedge/segmental resections :
– Segment V wedge resection.
– Segment VIII wedge resection.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT.
B. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy.
E. Whether any adjuvant chemotherapy was administered after the initial colon surgery.
F. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, operated for low rectal cancer 3 years ago (T3N1M0) after chemoradiotherapy. CEA 95 ng/mL. Liver MRI: lesion in segment II (2.5 cm) and micronodule segment V. RAS wild-type, MSS.
MDT Discussion: Metachronous metastases, potentially curable, negative extra-hepatic workup.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront: Both hepatic lesions are small (2.5 cm in segment II and a micronodule in segment V) and can be removed with limited anatomical or non‑anatomical resections while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. No extra‑hepatic disease is identified, and the patient’s performance status is not reported as limiting. Therefore the liver metastases are amenable to immediate surgical resection without prerequisite down‑staging therapy.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Confirm baseline assessment: complete blood count, liver panel, coagulation profile, indocyanine‑green clearance (or equivalent) and volumetric CT/MRI to verify that the future liver remnant will be ≥30 % in a 70‑year‑old.  
• Proceed to hepatic surgery: perform a segment II wedge/segmentectomy (or left lateral segmentectomy if needed for margin) and a segment V wedge or segmentectomy, aiming for R0 margins (>1 cm when feasible). Intra‑operative ultrasound should be used to locate the micronodule and exclude additional occult lesions.  
• Post‑operative pathology: assess margin status, tumor grade, and confirm RAS wild‑type status of metastases.  
• Adjuvant systemic therapy: given the high pre‑operative CEA (95 ng/mL) and prior rectal cancer, administer 6 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab). Because the tumor is RAS wild‑type and MSS, anti‑EGFR agents could be considered if future progression occurs, but are not required in the adjuvant setting.  
• Surveillance: CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the liver and pelvis every 6 months, and colonoscopic evaluation per standard colorectal cancer follow‑up guidelines.

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Exact size and radiologic characteristics of the segment V micronodule (to confirm suitability for limited resection).  
• Quantitative liver function assessment and future liver remnant volume calculation.  
• Patient’s current performance status and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve, frailty).  
• Details of any prior systemic chemotherapy regimens and interval since last treatment.  
These data would solidify the safety of immediate resection and guide peri‑operative chemotherapy planning.
Reference:

• Given the metachronous presentation after a long disease-free interval and limited liver involvement, immediate surgical resection is appropriate.

• Initiate adjuvant doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX).
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy according to MDT decision.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, history of left colectomy for T4N2 tumor, in remission for 2 years. Surveillance: CEA 430 ng/mL. FDG-PET: three bilobar liver lesions, 2-3 cm, no other foci. BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Metachronous liver recurrence, potentially resectable after discussion.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: Bilobar disease with three lesions 2‑3 cm each could be surgically cleared, but definitive feasibility depends on (a) quantitative assessment of future liver remnant (FLR) volume and functional reserve, and (b) the relationship of the lesions to major vascular structures. Without this information a safe upfront resection cannot be guaranteed; therefore prior evaluation (volumetry ± portal vein embolization) is required before surgery can be planned.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Baseline work‑up: complete blood count, liver panel, coagulation profile, indocyanine‑green clearance or 99mTc‑mebrofenin hepatobiliary scintigraphy, contrast‑enhanced liver MRI or CT for precise lesion mapping and volumetry, assessment of performance status and comorbidities.  
2. Initiate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months to (i) treat micrometastatic disease, (ii) assess tumor biology via CEA trend, and (iii) potentially downsize lesions.  
3. Restaging imaging after chemotherapy: repeat PET/CT or MRI to evaluate response, confirm absence of extra‑hepatic disease, and re‑measure FLR.  
4. If FLR is <30 % in a normal liver (or <40 % in a steatotic/cirrhotic liver), schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy.  
5. Surgical plan based on post‑PVE/response imaging:  
   - If all lesions become amenable to a single‑stage anatomic or non‑anatomic resection with adequate FLR, proceed to simultaneous resection (e.g., right hepatectomy plus segmental left‑lobe resection).  
   - If not, adopt a two‑stage hepatectomy: first stage resect lesions confined to one lobe (or perform PVE), allow hypertrophy, then second‑stage clearance of remaining lesions.  
6. Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (same regimen) for 3–6 months, adjusted to postoperative recovery and pathology (margin status, nodal involvement).  
7. Ongoing surveillance: CEA every 3 months, cross‑sectional imaging at 6‑month intervals.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume and functional assessment (ICG clearance or hepatobiliary scintigraphy).  
- Detailed anatomic location of each hepatic lesion relative to hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and biliary ducts.  
- Presence of underlying liver disease (steatosis, fibrosis, cirrhosis) and portal hypertension.  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- Baseline laboratory values (bilirubin, albumin, INR, platelet count).  
- Exact timing and results of any prior adjuvant therapy after the primary colectomy.

The patient presents with three metachronous bilobar liver metastases (2–3 cm) without evidence of extrahepatic disease. Although distributed in both lobes, the limited number and size of lesions suggest that parenchymal-sparing resections could achieve R0 margins while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited bilobar metachronous metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to precisely define the segmental distribution and vascular/biliary relationships of the lesions and a chest CT scan.

B. Consider peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the high CEA level (430 ng/mL), a 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) is advisable to treat micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.
• KRAS status is unknown
• BRAF wild-type does not modify the surgical indication.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

D. Surgical management after restaging
• If stability or response is observed, perform parenchymal-sparing resections / imaging guided ablation of the three lesions guided by intra-operative ultrasound.
• Depending on distribution, this may involve combined wedge resections or a staged approach if required to preserve liver volume.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of the three lesions on MRI with detailed vascular and biliary relationships of each lesion.
B. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
C. Histologic differentiation grade of the original colon tumor.
D. Details of any prior adjuvant chemotherapy received after the initial colectomy.
E. chest CT scan.
