Case_Content:
Woman, 55 years old, left colon cancer, multiple bilobar metastases at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 2100 ng/mL, BRAF wild-type, HER2 amplified.
MDT Discussion: Particular molecular profile, possible sensitivity to an anti-HER2 approach.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- Multiple bilobar liver metastases are present, but the CT report does not specify number, size, segmental distribution, relationship to major vascular structures, or future liver remnant volume.  
- Absence of data on extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes) precludes definitive judgment.  
- Conversion therapy (systemic chemotherapy combined with HER2‑directed agents) is required to attempt downsizing before a curative‑intent liver resection can be planned.  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic therapy with a HER2‑targeted regimen (e.g., trastuzumab + pertuzumab or trastuzumab‑deruxtecan) combined with a standard doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX).  
- Assess response after 2–3 months with high‑resolution liver MRI and PET‑CT to evaluate lesion shrinkage, new lesions, and extra‑hepatic spread.  
- If imaging shows sufficient tumor regression and a ≥30 % future liver remnant can be preserved, proceed to surgical planning:  
   • Perform volumetric CT or MRI to calculate future liver remnant; if inadequate, schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS.  
   • Plan hepatic resection aiming for R0 margins; decide between simultaneous colon and liver resection (if patient fitness and operative risk acceptable) or staged approach (colon first, then liver).  
- Continue HER2‑directed therapy peri‑operatively as tolerated; resume postoperative systemic therapy (same regimen) for at least 6 months as adjuvant treatment.  
- Monitor CEA and imaging every 3 months during the first year, then every 6 months.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Exact number, size, and segmental location of each liver metastasis.  
- Relationship of lesions to hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and biliary structures.  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume and baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, platelets, ICG clearance).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung nodules, peritoneal implants, distant lymph nodes).  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities affecting surgical risk.  
- KRAS/NRAS mutation status (relevant for anti‑EGFR considerations).  
- Baseline cardiac function (for HER2‑targeted therapy).  
- Detailed colon tumor staging (T stage, nodal involvement) and whether obstruction or bleeding is present.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with multiple bilobar liver metastases and very high CEA (2100 ng/mL) in the context of a left colon cancer with HER2 amplification and BRAF wild-type status. The tumor burden and bilobar distribution preclude the possibility of achieving a complete R0 resection while preserving an adequate future liver remnant at this stage. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable after major conversion.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships and a chest CT scan
• Given the high CEA level (2100 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Consider short peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the elevated CEA (2100 ng/mL) and HER2 positivity, a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative systemic therapy adapted to the molecular profile should be considered to treat micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.
• HER2-positive colorectal cancer (CRC), found in 2–6% of cases (mainly RAS wild-type and left-sided), is treated with targeted therapies like trastuzumab combined with tucatinib or trastuzumab deruxtecan. 

C. Radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2–3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Surgical management after restaging
• If disease remains controlled, perform ultrasound-guided left lateral sectoriectomy (rection of segments II and III) aiming for R0 margins.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

E. Surgical management of the primary tumor
• After recovery, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

G. If disease remains extensive
• Continue systemic and targeted therapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented management according to MDT.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Precise segmental distribution of the 2 lesions within the left liver and detailed vascular/biliary relationship of the liver lesion – essential to confirm that a non anatomic resection will achieve clear margins without compromising hepatic inflow/outflow.  
B. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA

Case_Content:
Man, 62 years old, T3N1M1 upper rectal tumor, liver metastases (3-5 cm) with contact with IVC and right hepatic vein at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 580 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Complex central metastases, discussion on combined approach or venous reconstruction.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The hepatic lesions are centrally located and abut the inferior vena cava and right hepatic vein, indicating that a standard anatomic resection would require major vascular reconstruction. Feasibility depends on (a) achieving an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) after resection and (b) confirming that the primary upper rectal cancer can be controlled (neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy) before or in conjunction with liver surgery. These prerequisites must be addressed before a definitive surgical plan can be made, thus the case is classified as “Potentially resectable.”

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) to assess tumor biology, obtain disease control, and potentially downsize the liver metastases.  
- Concurrently deliver long‑course neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for the upper rectal T3N1 tumor (45‑50 Gy with capecitabine or 5‑FU).  
- After 8‑12 weeks, restage with high‑resolution liver MRI (including hepatobiliary contrast) and triphasic CT to evaluate response of hepatic lesions, relationship to IVC/RHV, and calculate FLR volume. Include CT volumetry and indocyanine‑green clearance if liver function is borderline.  
- If FLR ≥30 % (≥40 % in steatotic or compromised liver) and vascular involvement is limited to abutment (no transmural invasion), plan curative‑intent hepatic resection with IVC/RHV reconstruction (using autologous vein graft, cryopreserved IVC segment, or prosthetic conduit as appropriate).  
- Decide on sequencing:  
   • Liver‑first approach if hepatic disease is the limiting factor, performing the complex hepatectomy with venous reconstruction, followed by recovery and then low anterior resection (or transanal TME) for the rectal primary.  
   • Alternatively, a simultaneous approach can be considered only if the patient’s performance status is excellent, operative time can be limited (<10 h), and intra‑operative blood loss is anticipated to be manageable.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy to complete a total of 6‑8 months of systemic therapy, adjusting regimen based on response and molecular profile (KRAS/BRAF, MSI).  
- Ongoing CEA monitoring and imaging (CT or MRI every 3‑4 months) for early detection of recurrence.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Exact number, size, and lobar distribution of all liver metastases.  
- Detailed imaging description of the depth of IVC and right hepatic vein involvement (abutment vs invasion).  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume and baseline liver function (bilirubin, ICG‑R15, Child‑Pugh).  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG), comorbidities, and cardiopulmonary reserve.  
- Molecular profile of the primary tumor (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI status).  
- Current trend of CEA levels and any prior systemic therapy received.  
- Presence or absence of other extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., lung, peritoneum).  
These data are essential to finalize resectability assessment and to tailor the operative plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with centrally located liver metastases (3–5 cm) in contact with the IVC and the right hepatic vein in the setting of an upper rectal T3N1 tumor, without reported extrahepatic disease. Although the number of lesions is not specified as excessive, the venous involvement makes a standard parenchymal-sparing R0 resection unsafe without complex vascular control or reconstruction. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable only after tumor downsizing and expert HPB / vascular reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvis MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships.
• Given the high CEA level (580 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Mandatory induction systemic therapy
• Initiate 2–3 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• The objective is tumor downsizing and reduction of venous contact.

C. Expert vascular restaging
• Repeat high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of lesions to the IVC and right hepatic vein.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Multidisciplinary evaluation with complex surgery to assess feasibility of venous reconstruction if required or right hepatomy including en-bloc resection of the right hepatic vein according to the future liver remnant.

D. Surgical management if feasibility is confirmed
• If regression occurs or venous reconstruction is deemed feasible, plan an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection with the aim of R0 margin.
• Anticipate possible IVC and/or hepatic vein reconstruction.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.

E. Surgical management after restaging : management of the rectal primary (oncologic priority)
• Given the T3N1 rectal cancer, long-course radiotherapy is appropriate to optimize local control and allow coordinated surgical planning 
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvis MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : with strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery, using a staged or synchronous strategy : oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

F. If disease remains extensive
• Continue systemic and targeted therapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented management according to MDT.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Precise extent and depth of contact with the IVC and right hepatic vein on MRI.
B. Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, and circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI influencing surgical approach and anastomotic risk
C. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the three liver lesions on MRI.
D. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
E. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy and long-course pelvic radiotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
F. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
G. Trend and quantification of circulating tumor cells over time.

Case_Content:
Woman, 67 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, multiple liver metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan and normal CEA at 3 ng/mL. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Biological discordance, question regarding the utility of CEA follow-up in this profile.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The presence of multiple liver metastases raises the possibility of curative resection, but critical information required to determine technical feasibility is missing. Specifically, we need:  
- Exact number, size, and segmental distribution of hepatic lesions  
- Assessment of future liver remnant (FLR) volume and function  
- Evaluation for any extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., pulmonary or peritoneal metastases) that would preclude a liver‑only approach  
- Patient’s performance status, comorbidities, and baseline liver biochemistry  

Without these data we cannot confirm that an upfront hepatectomy is safe, nor can we deem the disease unresectable; therefore the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending completion of the missing assessments.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Complete staging work‑up  
   - Perform a liver‑specific MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to delineate lesion number, size, and relationship to vascular structures.  
   - Obtain high‑resolution chest CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out occult pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic disease.  
   - Calculate FLR using volumetric software; assess liver function (ICG clearance, bilirubin, albumin).  
2. Initiate systemic conversion chemotherapy  
   - Preferred regimen: FOLFOXIRI plus bevacizumab (if patient is fit) or FOLFOX plus bevacizumab, given KRAS‑mutated, BRAF‑wild‑type disease.  
   - Aim for maximal tumor shrinkage while monitoring for toxicity; reassess after 2–3 months (or after 6–8 cycles).  
3. Re‑evaluate resectability after systemic therapy  
   - Repeat liver MRI and CT to document radiologic response.  
   - If FLR remains inadequate, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy.  
4. Surgical plan (contingent on response)  
   - If hepatic disease becomes resectable and no extra‑hepatic disease is present, proceed with curative intent. Options:  
     • Simultaneous right hemicolectomy and liver resection (if extent of liver surgery is limited and FLR adequate).  
     • Staged approach: primary colon resection first, followed by liver resection after recovery, especially if major hepatectomy is required.  
   - Aim for R0 margins on both primary and liver lesions; use intra‑operative ultrasound to guide resection.  
5. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
   - Post‑operative continuation of bevacizumab‑containing regimen for up to 6 months, then transition to maintenance (e.g., fluoropyrimidine ± bevacizumab) per current guidelines.  
6. Surveillance  
   - Given low baseline CEA, rely on imaging (contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI) every 3–6 months rather than CEA alone for disease monitoring.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Detailed hepatic lesion characteristics (number, maximal diameter, segmental location, vascular involvement).  
- Quantitative assessment of future liver remnant volume and functional reserve.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic metastases beyond the liver (lung nodules, peritoneal disease).  
- Patient’s ECOG performance status and comorbidity profile (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, AST/ALT, albumin, INR, ICG clearance if available).  
- Results of high‑resolution chest imaging (CT or PET‑CT).  
- MSI/MMR status (relevant for immunotherapy considerations).  
- Planned or ongoing systemic therapy regimen and response assessments.

• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvis MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships.

• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2–3 months to evaluate response.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgery (exceptional)
• Surgical re-evaluation could be considered only if a major radiologic response occurs with significant reduction in tumor burden allowing parenchymal-sparing resections.

E. Surgical management of the primary tumor
• Perform right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.

F. Postoperative therapy 
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.

G. Surveillance considerations
• Imaging-based surveillance is essential, as CEA is not a reliable marker in this patient.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Precise segmental distribution of all the lesions within the left and right liver and detailed vascular/biliary relationship of the liver lesion – essential to confirm that a non anatomic resection will achieve clear margins without compromising hepatic inflow/outflow.  
B. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression)

Case_Content:

Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
The bilobar liver lesions (1.5‑3 cm) are within a size range that can be cleared with parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy, but the case lacks critical information needed to confirm that an R0 resection with an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) is feasible. A dedicated liver MRI with volumetry, assessment of lesion proximity to major vessels/ducts, baseline liver function (bilirubin, ICG clearance, Child‑Pugh), and overall performance status are required before declaring the disease resectable upfront. Until these data are obtained, the lesions must be considered potentially resectable, pending down‑staging or confirmation of technical feasibility.

Case_Content:
Woman, 69 years old, T4N2M1 transverse colon cancer, seven liver metastases at the abdominal CT scan, CEA 1150 ng/mL, NRAS Q61R mutation.
MDT Discussion: Specific NRAS molecular profile, no sensitivity to anti-EGFR.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The presence of seven liver metastases raises concern for bilobar disease and may limit the future liver remnant (FLR). Definitive classification requires precise information on lesion size, segmental distribution, proximity to major vascular structures, and volumetric assessment of the FLR. Without these data, we cannot confirm that an R0 resection is feasible upfront, but conversion to resectability is possible after down‑staging and/or liver‑volume augmentation.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Obtain a high‑resolution liver MRI with diffusion‑weighted imaging and perform 3‑dimensional volumetry to define lesion distribution and calculate FLR.  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy tailored to NRAS‑mutated colorectal cancer: FOLFOXIRI (or FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab, given the lack of anti‑EGFR efficacy. Plan 3–4 cycles before first restaging.  
- Restage with contrast‑enhanced CT/MRI after the initial chemotherapy course. Assess tumor response (RECIST), re‑evaluate FLR, and determine whether sufficient down‑staging has occurred.  
- If FLR remains inadequate (<30 % in a normal liver, <40 % in steatotic/cirrhotic liver) but disease is responding, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy.  
- Plan a two‑stage hepatectomy or a single‑stage extended resection depending on lesion distribution after hypertrophy:  
   • Stage 1: PVE (or ALPPS) ± resection of lesions confined to one lobe if feasible.  
   • Stage 2 (4–6 weeks later): definitive liver resection aiming for R0 margins, preserving ≥30 % functional liver.  
- Address the primary transverse colon tumor:  
   • If symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) or if liver disease is controlled, perform a colectomy either before liver surgery or simultaneously during the second liver stage, depending on operative risk and patient performance status.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant systemic therapy (continuation of the same regimen or switch to maintenance bevacizumab) for at least 6 months, adjusted to postoperative recovery and pathology.  
- Throughout treatment, monitor CEA trends and repeat imaging every 2–3 months to detect early recurrence.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Detailed liver lesion characteristics: size of each metastasis, exact segmental location, bilobar vs unilobar involvement, relationship to hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and biliary ducts.  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume and baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, platelet count, indocyanine‑green clearance if available).  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky), comorbidities, and cardiopulmonary reserve.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung nodules, peritoneal implants, distant lymph nodes) on staging PET‑CT or chest CT.  
- Baseline laboratory values: liver enzymes, albumin, renal function, coagulation profile.  
- Any prior systemic therapy or radiotherapy received for the primary tumor.

Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with seven liver metastases in the setting of a T4N2 transverse colon cancer and markedly elevated CEA (1150 ng/mL). The number of lesions and likely bilobar distribution make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not feasible at this stage. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered unresectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships of all lesions.
• Given the high CEA level (1150 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Systemic therapy as primary strategy (mandatory)
• Initiate systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• The NRAS Q61R mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• The objective is tumor downsizing and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2–3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgery (exceptional)
• Surgical re-evaluation could be considered only if a major radiologic and biologic response occurs with significant reduction in number and size of lesions allowing parenchymal-sparing resections with R0 margin.

E. Management of primary tumor
• If symptomatic or if consideration of intra arterial chemotherapy, perform extended right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right and transverse colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

G. If disease remains extensive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented management according to MDT.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Precise relationship of each lesion to the hepatic vein confluence on MRI.
B. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of the three lesions.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Confirmation of absence of extrahepatic disease on full staging.

G. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.

Case_Content:
Man, 70 years old, left colon tumor, three liver metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 200 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSS. MRI: invasion of the hepatic vein confluence.
MDT Discussion: Superior vascular involvement, significant technical risk, volume to be assessed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – The hepatic vein confluence involvement creates a high‑risk technical scenario and the future liver remnant (FLR) has not been quantified. Adequate FLR volume and functional reserve must be confirmed (or augmented with portal vein embolization) before a safe hepatic resection can be planned.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) as a neoadjuvant down‑staging regimen, given the high tumor burden (CEA 200 ng/mL) and need to assess tumor biology.  
- After 2–3 months, repeat high‑resolution liver MRI with volumetry and intra‑hepatic vascular mapping to:  
   • Determine FLR percentage (target >30 % in normal liver, >40 % if steatosis/fibrosis).  
   • Clarify the extent of hepatic vein confluence invasion and feasibility of reconstruction.  
- If FLR is insufficient, perform portal vein embolization (PVE) of the liver segments to be resected and re‑image after 2–3 weeks to confirm hypertrophy.  
- Re‑evaluate resectability after chemotherapy ± PVE:  
   • If all three metastases can be removed with negative margins while preserving adequate FLR, plan a combined or staged approach.  
   • Preferred: staged resection – first resect the primary left‑sided colon cancer (laparoscopic or open segmental colectomy) followed by hepatic surgery after systemic therapy response.  
   • Hepatic surgery: consider extended right hepatectomy with hepatic vein reconstruction (e.g., interposition graft or venous patch) or ex‑vivo liver resection with autotransplantation if reconstruction is not feasible intra‑operatively. Use intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm margins.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy to complete a total of 6 months of systemic therapy, adjusting regimen based on response and tolerance.  
- Ongoing surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3–6 months.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Quantitative FLR volume and liver function (bilirubin, ICG clearance, Child‑Pugh, MELD).  
- Exact anatomical relationship of each metastasis to hepatic veins, portal branches, and biliary ducts.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., lung, peritoneum).  
- Performance status and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- Status of the primary tumor (symptomatic, obstructive, already resected).  
- Detailed histopathology of the primary (grade, lymphovascular invasion).  
- Baseline renal function and hematologic parameters to assess chemotherapy tolerance.

Case_Content:
Woman, 56 years old, right T3N1M1 colon cancer, four liver metastases (3-5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 780 ng/mL, non-V600E BRAF mutation (D594G).
MDT Discussion: Atypical BRAF mutation, intermediate prognosis, bilobar liver involvement.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- Four bilobar metastases measuring 3‑5 cm each raise concern for an insufficient future liver remnant (FLR) after an anatomic or parenchymal‑sparing resection.  
- No volumetric or functional liver data (FLR percentage, ICG clearance, bilirubin, portal hypertension) are provided, which are decisive to confirm that a curative hepatectomy can be performed while preserving ≥30 % functional liver in a non‑cirrhotic patient.  
- Therefore resection is possible only after obtaining the missing liver‑volume/functional information and, if needed, after down‑staging with systemic therapy or portal vein embolization.  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy aimed at tumor down‑staging and early control of micrometastatic disease: preferred regimen FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab (or FOLFOX + bevacizumab) given the BRAF D594G mutation and intermediate prognosis.  
- Re‑evaluate after 2–3 months with contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI and obtain quantitative liver volumetry (CT‑based or MRI‑based) to calculate FLR.  
- If FLR ≥30 % (or ≥40 % in case of steatosis/chemotherapy‑associated liver injury) and all lesions are resectable with negative margins, proceed to liver surgery:  
   • Consider a parenchymal‑sparing, staged hepatectomy (e.g., first resection of lesions in one lobe, portal vein embolization of the contralateral lobe if FLR inadequate, followed by second‑stage resection).  
   • If FLR remains marginal, evaluate ALPPS or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy.  
- Primary colon tumor:  
   • If symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) resect colon first, then address liver disease after recovery.  
   • If asymptomatic, simultaneous colon and liver resection can be contemplated only after confirming that the combined operative time and physiologic stress are acceptable; otherwise, stage colon resection after hepatic clearance.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant therapy: complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy; consider adding targeted agents (e.g., EGFR inhibitor) only if KRAS/NRAS wild‑type and appropriate for non‑V600E BRAF mutation.  
- Ongoing surveillance: CEA monitoring, imaging every 3–6 months for the first 2 years.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Quantitative liver volumetry (FLR %).  
- Baseline liver function (bilirubin, albumin, ICG clearance, presence of steatosis or fibrosis).  
- Detailed segmental location of each metastasis (to plan parenchymal‑sparing resections).  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- KRAS/NRAS mutation status and microsatellite instability status.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease not described on current imaging.  
- Patient’s preferences regarding staged versus simultaneous surgery.

From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable.

• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships of all lesions.

• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2-3 months to evaluate response.

Case_Content:
Man, 65 years old, left T4N2M1 colon cancer, six liver metastases (2-4 cm)at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 320 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSS. Positive circulating tumor cells detected.
MDT Discussion: Presence of circulating tumor cells despite no visible extension, prognostic value discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: Six hepatic lesions measuring 2‑4 cm could be surgically removed if an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved, but the current information does not specify lesion distribution (unilobar vs bilobar), relationship to major vascular structures, baseline liver function, or volumetric data. These missing pieces are decisive for determining whether a curative hepatectomy is feasible now or after portal vein embolization (PVE). Therefore the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending further anatomic and functional assessment.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy with a triplet regimen (FOLFOXIRI) combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab) because the tumor is left‑sided and RAS wild‑type.  
- Treat for 3–4 months, monitoring CEA trend and radiologic response.  
- Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast and volumetric analysis after chemotherapy to:  
   • Confirm number, size, and exact location of all metastases.  
   • Calculate FLR; if FLR <30 % (or <40 % in steatotic liver) plan portal vein embolization of the lobe to be resected.  
- Re‑stage disease after imaging:  
   • If all lesions are now amenable to complete (R0) resection with adequate FLR, schedule curative surgery.  
   • Preferred operative sequence: simultaneous colon resection (left hemicolectomy) and liver resection if the combined procedure is expected to be <5 h, blood loss <500 ml, and the patient’s performance status permits. Otherwise, adopt a staged approach (colon first, then liver after recovery).  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (same regimen or continuation of the pre‑operative regimen) for at least 3 months, adjusted to pathology (margin status, nodal burden).  
- If imaging after chemotherapy shows progression or new extra‑hepatic disease, shift to a non‑curative systemic strategy and consider clinical trial enrollment.

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Detailed hepatic lesion map (unilobar vs bilobar, proximity to major vessels/ducts).  
- Quantitative liver function (ICG clearance, bilirubin, AST/ALT, platelet count).  
- Volumetric assessment of future liver remnant.  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- Presence or absence of other extra‑hepatic metastases (lung, peritoneum) on full staging (CT chest, PET‑CT).  
- Baseline nutritional status and baseline CEA trend.  

These data are essential to finalize resectability and to tailor the surgical plan.
